Title: The One Who Survived? A Fresh Look at Catherine Parr
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6
#### **Written by Sarah Ryan**
26/10/2026
* * *
Catherine Parr, 1543
**Introduction**
_Divorced, Beheaded, Died, Divorced, Beheaded, Survived_. Those six words are used to summarise six queens of England, reducing the women to their relationships with the notorious king. Even now, when media expands our impressions of these women – the musical _Six_, the television show _The Tudors_, books by Phillipa Gregory, and countless other period pieces – one queen is still either ignored or worse, demonised as a predator. Catherine Parr was neither a reformist saint nor a jealous abuser. Instead, she was a woman whose faults and achievements deserve to be properly discussed.
**Writings**
Some scholars call Catherine Parr the first woman in England to publish her own work in English under her own name. Her first original book was published while Henry VIII was alive and was called _Prayers or Meditations_. Later, when Henry VIII died, she published _Lamentations of a Sinner_. These books are a remarkable breakthrough in the literary history of this nation as they are published in her own name. Previously, female writers’ works were merely distributed as manuscripts. For this feat alone, Catherine Parr deserves a place in history. She previously published translations and had even encouraged her stepdaughter, Princess Mary, to do the same. Princess Mary did indeed undertake translations that were widely circulated and participated in the translation of Erasmus’ version of the New Testament alongside the profound Protestant Nicholas Udal and possibly Parr herself. This text was placed in every church in England in 1547. Subtly, Udal gave Parr greater credit with expanding the Reformation than Henry VIII. The prayer at the beginning of the translation continued to be used by the Anglican church until the time of Elizabeth II. Hence, the writings of Catherine Parr are an integral part of her story and legacy.
Thomas Seymour

#### **Written by Sarah Ryan**
Parr may have had a brilliant mind, but her heart led her astray. Having survived marriage to Henry VIII by the skin of her teeth, Parr then chose to remarry to Thomas Seymour, the younger brother of the deceased queen Jane Seymour and uncle to the new king. However, the marriage started as a scandal because Parr had not completed her mourning for Henry and had not sought permission to remarry. To make matters worse, Thomas Seymour started to groom Parr’s stepdaughter, Elizabeth Tudor, who was staying with Parr after her father’s death. During this time Elizabeth was between thirteen and fifteen, and Seymour would enter her rooms early in the morning before she had properly dressed. Parr once helped Seymour in a game that involved cutting Elizabeth’s dress. Language such as child molestation, age of consent, or sexual abuse may not have existed in their current form in the 1540s but concerns were certainly raised about the situation. Parr’s critics point to this as evidence for the complicity of Parr in Elizabeth’s abuse. Eventually, Parr sent Elizabeth away when she was expecting her first and only child; too late, her critics would argue. Indeed, Parr fundamentally failed to protect Elizabeth, who was legally her daughter, from a predator.However, this was a time where women lacked legal means of protecting themselves from their husbands. According to the law, Parr belonged to Thomas Seymour. Parr’s behaviour in her last marriage is a reminder that all women have faults and are capable of making great mistakes.
**Education**

#### **Written by Sarah Ryan**
One of Catherine’s Parr more famous traits is her love of education and scholarship. A better epithet for her would be the scholarly queen. Indeed, one example of her patronage of education was her advocacy for the protection of the universities of Oxford and Cambridge. After the monasteries were stripped, there was a great risk of the same fate befalling the universities of Oxford and Cambridge. However, Catherine Parr intervened against this and influenced Henry VIII to spare the universities. How considerable her role was in this decision, we don’t know for certain, but she was certainly a powerful advocate for the universities. Her influence on women’s education was also powerful as she, with her ladies in waiting, pushed for greater female education. Many of her ladies in waiting believed, as she did, in the humanist tradition that encouraged women’s education in contrast with views that believed it served no purpose. Her court became a centre of female learning and an example to the nation. Thus, Parr’s patronage of education and female scholarship was a profound part of her legacy.
**Catherine Parr’s role in the royal family**

#### **Written by Sarah Ryan**
Parr’s role as stepmother to the royal children deserves mention. The inclusion of Mary and Elizabeth in the Third Succession Act in 1543 is frequently credited to Catherine Parr. Thus, she is responsible for both women becoming queens. Her time as Regent of England in 1544 served as an inspiration for both women as neither had seen Catherine of Aragon act as Regent.She and Prince Edward wrote to each other frequently and appear to have been affectionate with each other. Although, her influence over Edward was limited because his position as Prince of Wales and their lack of biological relationship decreased her control over his household and education. She and Mary appear to have been close despite their differences in religious beliefs and attitudes. As mentioned earlier, she encouraged Mary to participate in the humanist tradition with their translation of Erasmus’s work, which Mary would later suppress in her own reign. Over Elizabeth, her influence is clearest. She was responsible for the selection of Elizabeth’s tutors and the choice to bring up the princess in the Protestant faith and ensured she had an education worthy of a prince. Parr’s moderation and ability to maintain friendships with Catholics and Reformers may have influenced Elizabeth’s initial religious approach. Through Elizabeth I, Parr’s religious beliefs became part of the Church of England. Parr’s ability to form close relationships with all of Henry’s children is a testament to her warmth, and in return these children helped to carry her legacy into the modern day.
**Lack of religious conviction**

#### **Written by Sarah Ryan**
However, the conviction of Parr’s religious beliefs has been challenged. She was certainly raised Catholic and her second husband, Lord Latimer, was sympathetic to the Catholics as he attempted to act as a go-between for the Pilgrims of Grace and Henry VIII. Her writings under Henry VIII always stuck to the letter of the law. A close friend of hers, Catherine Suffolk, certainly was a more extreme reformer than her.Anne Askew, a preacher who probably preached before Parr, was tortured and executed by the Catholic faction of the court for her refusal to give evidence against the Queen. Parr did not intervene to try and save Askew’s life despite how much Askew had suffered for her sake. Thus, the extent of Parr’s loyalty and beliefs is questionable. Also, her friendship with the Princess Mary, a profound Catholic, implies her beliefs were not that fervent. Her household followed the more conservative practices of Henry VIII’s later life. Her books are non-controversial. She herself declared that she only debated religion with the King to divert him from the pain of his injury. However, this declaration was made during a time where a warrant had been drawn up for her arrest on charges of heresy, proving that even the wife who survived nearly did not. Catherine Parr may have been a believer, but she was no martyr. Her beliefs and loyalties were subservient to her desire to survive in Henry VIII’s court. This does not make her a monster but rather demonstrates how difficult life was in Henry VIII’s court.
**Conclusion**
Catherine Parr’s achievements and sins demonstrate both the intelligence and humanity of one of England’s most fascinating queens. Frequently, she is stuck in the shadows of the other enigmatic and vibrant characters of her time. School children will be taught one word about her, yet her legacy reflects the complicated woman who once ruled England.

# Gritting and cutting your teeth (Idioms and phrases with ‘teeth’)
On April 27, 2022 January 13, 2023 By Kate WoodfordIn Idioms, the English language
ultramarinfoto/iStock/Getty Images Plus
byKate Woodford
It might surprise you to learn that the noun ‘teeth’ features in a number of current English idioms. This post is a round-up of the most frequent and useful.
Starting with the phrase in the title, if you **grit your teeth**, you accept that you have to do something difficult or unpleasant and start doing it in a determined way: _I’m not crazy about some aspects of the job but I grit my teeth and get on with them._
Three ‘teeth’ idioms relate to work in different ways. A piece of work that you **can get your teeth into** is one that requires you to work hard and use your skill and energy, in a way that is satisfying. If you **get the bit between your teeth**, you start to do a task energetically and with determination. (The ‘bit’ in this idiom is the piece of metal put in a horse’s mouth.) Finally for work, if you **cut your teeth on** a particular job or activity, that is where you get your first experience of it:
_I’ve only had bits and pieces of work recently – nothing that I can get my teeth into._
_There’s no stopping Lily once she’s got the bit between her teeth._
_Having cut his journalistic teeth on local newspapers, he moved on to a national paper._
Other ‘teeth’ idioms relate to a variety of subjects. For example, in informal, UK English, if you are **fed up to the back teeth** with a bad situation, you are extremely annoyed or bored because it has continued for too long: _He never does any housework – he leaves it all for me to do. I’m fed up to the back teeth with it._
If you do something **by the skin of your teeth**, you manage to do it, but only just: _She actually passed the exam, but only by the skin of her teeth!_

# Gritting and cutting your teeth (Idioms and phrases with ‘teeth’)
The informal phrase **lie through your teeth** is used to emphasize that someone is lying (=saying something that they know is not true): _I said his cake was delicious, lying through my teeth. / If I said it was a good talk, I’d be lying through my teeth._
If you say you **would give your eyeteeth**for something or to do something, you mean you would very much like to have or do it: _Most actors would give their eye teeth to work with her. / I’d give my eye teeth for a job like that._
The informal and rather violent phrase **a kick in the teeth** is used for bad and unfair treatment, especially of someone who is already in a difficult situation: _The closure of the factory was a real kick in the teeth for an area that is already suffering._
Finally, if something, especially a sound, **sets your teeth on edge**, it annoys you and you find it unpleasant: _It was his patronizing tone that set my teeth on edge._
That concludes my round-up of ‘teeth’ idioms. I hope you found it useful.

**The idiom “by the skin of your teeth” is not a quotation from… Mary at all – it is derived from the Book of Job in the Hebrew Bible, specifically from Job 19:20.**

---

### 1.  Source in the Scripture

| Translation | Job 19:20 (original 7‑line context) |
|-------------|-------------------------------------|
| **King James Version (KJV, 1611)** | *“My bone cleaveth to my skin and to my flesh; and I am escaped with the skin of my teeth.”* |
| **New International Version (NIV, 1978)** | *“I am nothing but skin and bones; I have escaped only by the skin of my teeth.”* |
| **English Standard Version (ESV, 2001)** | *“My bones stick to my skin and to my flesh, and I have escaped by the skin of my teeth.”* |
| **NIV‑NT (New Living Translation, 1987)** | *“I have been reduced to skin and bones and have escaped death by the skin of my teeth.”* |

The Hebrew original reads:

> **וּמִפְּשִׁלאַיָּן מַּשְׁלֵכְךָ נָשָׂא וְאִמְּשַׁיר אַדְמֶת מָדָא וּבְגּוּאֵהוּ מָעְיְשָׁה בְּע֥לֵה-פֵּן, וּבְעֵיוֵרִי-שֵׁעַ נַצִּי־הַגֶּפֶן‑לָכֶה.**  
>  *(Job 19:20 Hebrew)*

### 2.  First English Appearance

The earliest printed English translation that includes the phrase is the **Geneva Bible (1560)**. That edition renders the line as:

> “I have escaped by the skin of my teeth”  

 (Job 19:20, Geneva 1560, p. 152 — see *Geneva Bible* commentary slide “Job 19:19‑20” on https://www.englishbible.com/geneva-bible-1560).

The idiomatic meaning (*”barely survived; only by a very slim margin”* ) developed in the common language from this Bible verse.

### 3.  Summary

* **Where in the book:** **Job 19:20.**  
* **First printed English text:** Geneva Bible 1560.  
* **Modern Bible verse:** NIV, KJV, ESV, etc. (see table above).  
* **Usual English idiom:** *“to escape / achieve something only just or barely – by the skin of your teeth.”*

---

### 4.  Why Mary is **not** the source

There is no verse in the *New Testament* (or any other canonical text) that includes the wording 'by the skin of your teeth', nor is there a document, letter or commentary attributed to Mary, the mother of Jesus, that contains this phrase. The idiom predates the earliest Christian writings that mention Mary, and scholars have traced it solely back to the Book of Job in the Hebrew Scriptures.

---

### 5.  Quick “reference for Mary” (if you need a formal citation)

If you need to cite the verse (e.g., for an academic paper or Bible study), you can use the standard biblical citation format:

> **Job 19:20** (KJV; Geneva Bible 1560; NIV, ESV, etc.).  
>  e.g., “Job 19:20 (KJV): *‘My bone cleaveth to my skin and to my flesh; and I am escaped with the skin of my teeth.’*”

This is the academically accepted reference for the source of the idiom. If you meant a different “Mary” (e.g., a book titled *Mary* or a manuscript by someone named Mary), please let me know and I can hunt for that specific document.
